title: Engineering Better Evals: Scalable LLM Evaluation Pipelines That Work — Dat Ngo, Aman Khan, Arize

summary: Dat Ngo, Director of AI Solutions at Arize AI, delivers a technical talk on LLM evaluation pipelines at the AI Engineer World's Fair. He frames evals as signals within an observability workflow, emphasizing that LLM-as-a-judge is one tool among many. The eval toolbox includes encoder-only BERT models (10x cheaper, 1-2 orders of magnitude faster), user feedback, golden datasets, and code-based heuristics. Golden datasets can quantify and tune LLM-as-a-judge by checking whether it approximates trusted human labels. Two virtuous cycles exist: improving AI systems through eval signals and tuning the evals themselves. Ngo stresses iteration velocity as critical—four iterations per month versus two yields exponentially better products. He expands eval granularity from component-level to workflow-level to session-level, with control-flow evaluated first to enable conditional evals that save cost. A hot take: avoid out-of-box evals; customize heavily. Arize's AI co-pilot demonstrates AI evaluating AI. Agent evals focus on understanding failure modes across aggregate traces, with Arize's framework-agnostic agent graph supporting LangGraph, CrewAI, and handrolled code. Trajectory evals use golden datasets for expected paths, graded by LLM comparison or exact node matching. Online vs offline evals map to in-orchestration vs out-of-orchestration, with guardrails as system-two checks on system-one orchestration—fixing root causes in system one is preferable to adjusting guardrails. For distributed async systems, OpenTelemetry propagation solves cross-service tracing. Confidence scores come from log probabilities or classification probabilities. In closing, Ngo addresses automated prompt optimization: referencing DSPY's MIRO optimizer, which creates less fragile prompts spanning different models, and Arize's metaprompting capability—feeding input/output pairs and eval pass/fail results to an LLM to generate improved prompts automatically.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Dat Ngo introduces himself as an AI architect at Arize AI, the largest AI evals player, working with companies like Reddit and Duolingo. Duolingo runs about 20 evals per trace. He emphasizes keeping the talk technical rather than salesy.

sections.title: Observability and LLM Team Structure
sections.summary: Observability answers what a system is doing through traces, spans, and conversations. LLM teams split into platform teams (owning infrastructure like model gateways, caring about cost and latency) and application teams (building business-facing products, caring about evals). Different teams care about different metrics.

sections.title: Evals as Signal and LLM-as-a-Judge
sections.summary: Evals are a clever word for signal—discerning what works and what doesn't. LLM-as-a-judge is one tool where an LLM provides feedback on a process. For RAG, every arrow in the pipeline can be evaluated, such as checking retrieval relevance against the query. About half the room had used LLM-as-a-judge.

sections.title: Beyond LLM-as-a-Judge: The Eval Toolbox
sections.summary: Encoder-only BERT-type architectures are 10x cheaper and 1-2 orders of magnitude faster. User feedback is incredible signal but only ~30% had implemented it. Golden datasets represent human-graded quality and can be used to quantify and tune LLM-as-a-judge. Code-based heuristics (keyword matching, regex, JSON parsability) are infinitely cheaper for simple checks.

sections.title: Two Virtuous Cycles and Iteration Velocity
sections.summary: Two virtuous cycles: (1) collect data, run evals, discern signal, identify failures, update prompts/models/orchestration; (2) tune evals themselves by collecting eval failures and improving eval prompt templates. Iteration velocity is critical—four iterations per month versus two yields exponentially better products.

sections.title: Architecture Example: Booking.com Trip Planner
sections.summary: Booking.com's trip planner is a travel agent LLM driving revenue. Evals can be as complex as the application itself, with component-level evals possible within traces, especially in routing architectures.

sections.title: Multi-Granularity Evals and Customization Hot Take
sections.summary: Evals can zoom out from component-level to workflow-level (evaluating input/output of a larger workflow of LLM calls, API calls, heuristics) to control-flow-level. Conditional evals make sense: if control flow fails, don't eval downstream—it's probably wrong, saving cost. Session-level evals evaluate back-and-forth conversations (e.g., customer frustration). Ngo's hot take: don't use out-of-box evals—customize heavily, as the best teams in the world do.

sections.title: Arize AI Co-Pilot and AI Evaluating AI
sections.summary: Arize built an AI co-pilot whose purpose is to troubleshoot, observe, and build evals for AI systems. Ngo predicts that in 5-10 years, AI—not humans—will evaluate AI systems. The co-pilot has been out for about a year and is getting better.

sections.title: Agent Evaluation and Framework-Agnostic Agent Graph
sections.summary: Agent evals are far more complex with longer traces. The real question is not whether an agent is good or bad, but what failure modes exist. Arize's framework-agnostic agent graph (supporting LangGraph, CrewAI, handrolled code) shows pathing across aggregate traces, revealing tool-call distributions and dependency issues (e.g., component 4 depending on component 3). Understanding the distribution across all instantiations is key.

sections.title: Trajectory Evaluation for Agents
sections.summary: Trajectory evals use golden datasets for expected agent paths (e.g., start→agent→tool→agent). Two approaches: (1) pass actual and expected trajectories to an LLM for grading, or (2) check exact trajectory node matching. Ground truth isn't always needed—creative approaches include comparing node descriptions against expected trajectories or checking against possible paths using nested key-value pairs.

sections.title: Q&A: Online vs Offline Evals and Guardrails
sections.summary: Online vs offline evals map to in-orchestration vs out-of-orchestration. Guardrails (system two) protect orchestration (system one) but have costs: latency, complexity, and the common mistake of adjusting guardrails instead of fixing root causes in system one. Guardrails act like unit tests for known knowns; observability plus eval handles unknown distributions. Embedding-based guardrails can be 2 orders of magnitude shorter to mitigate latency.

sections.title: Q&A: Async Systems, OpenTelemetry, and Confidence Scores
sections.summary: For distributed async systems across services, containers, or Kubernetes pods, OpenTelemetry (OTEL) propagation solves cross-service tracing—Arize bet on OTEL 2.5 years ago. For confidence scores on evals: autoregressive models expose log probabilities (pseudo-confidence for single eval-token outputs), while encoder-only models provide classification probabilities. Multiple tools are used together to discern signal.

sections.title: Q&A: Automated Prompt Optimization and Closing
sections.summary: Final question concerns shortening the loop between customer feedback and prompt improvements. Ngo references DSPY's MIRO optimizer, which takes ~30 input/output pairs and creates less fragile prompts that span across different models (OpenAI, Gemini, etc.). Arize is releasing or has the ability to run prompt optimization via metaprompting—feeding input/output pairs and eval pass/fail data to an LLM that examines the original prompt and generates an improved version. Ngo invites attendees to continue conversations at the Arize booth.
